title: Six million
hookLine: six million Jews were murdered, alongside Roma, disabled people and many others

cards: A highway in Israel, mid-morning, traffic moving fast. Then a siren starts, long and steady, across the whole country at once. The cars slow and stop, right there in the lanes.
Drivers open their doors and step out and stand beside them, heads down. On sidewalks, in shops, in classrooms, people stand still. Nobody speaks.
Then the siren fades, and the cars start again. It's Yom HaShoah, the day of remembrance for the Holocaust. Today's word is the number they're standing for.

teach.h: THE JEWISH DEAD OF THE SHOAH.
teach.b: Six million. That is the number of Jews murdered in the Holocaust, as Yad Vashem and historians of the Shoah count them. Men and women, grandparents, babies.
Whole families, whole towns, whole ways of life. They were shot at the edges of pits, starved in ghettos, and murdered in camps built to kill. And they were not alone.

teach.h: ROMA, DISABLED PEOPLE, AND MANY OTHERS.
teach.b: The Nazis and their collaborators also murdered Roma and Sinti, disabled people, Polish civilians, Soviet prisoners of war, gay men, political prisoners and many others.
Remembering one group of the dead never erases another. A number that large is almost impossible to hold; the mind slides off it. Jewish tradition has a way of turning it around.

The Mishnah, in a passage about witnesses in a court where a life is at stake, teaches that one human being was created first, alone, so that we would learn this: whoever destroys a single soul is as if they destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves a single soul is as if they saved a whole world.
So the title is not one number. It is six million worlds, each one complete. And what do you say in front of that?
The Torah tells of Aaron, whose two sons died suddenly in the sanctuary. Moses speaks to him, and Aaron answers with nothing: "And Aaron held his peace."
Some readers hear that silence not as an absence of words, but as the only honest answer.
Silence is part of how the Holocaust is remembered too, as on that highway when the siren sounds.

how: On Yom HaShoah, Israel stops for a siren while people stand in silence, and Jewish communities elsewhere hold memorial services with candles, the reading of names and the memorial prayers.

games.q: the siren sounds on Yom HaShoah. you are driving on a highway in Israel. what do people do?
o: keep driving and turn on the radio.
stop, get out, and stand in silence beside the car.
pull off at the next exit.
games.why: the cars stop in the lanes, drivers step out and stand with heads down, and nobody speaks until the siren fades.

practice: Stand if you can, the way the drivers do, or sit, and keep a minute of silence.
Don't try to picture six million; let just one person be in the silence with you, a child, an old woman, a face from an old photo, one whole world, and then let the silence hold all the others.
If you pray, let the silence be your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Six million. The Jews murdered in the Holocaust, each one, as the Mishnah teaches, a whole world, remembered alongside the Roma, disabled people and all the others the Nazis killed. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: and Aaron held his peace, from Leviticus 10:3, the Torah's picture of silence in the face of loss.

carryVoice: Your line: each one a whole world. The silence holds what words can't. Take all the quiet you need.
